variants.name: C11 atomic flag polled at safe points
requires_features: a wakeup primitive (condition variable, queue or self-pipe)
variants.idiom_name: atomic_bool token + condition-variable or self-pipe wakeup, checked at safe points
variants.implementation_notes: C has no cancellation type, so the token is hand-written: an atomic_bool (C11 <stdatomic.h>) owned by the caller, plus a wakeup primitive - a cnd_t/mtx_t pair, a queue, or a self-pipe - so a waiter blocked in poll/select is woken when the flag flips and re-checks it. The classic object structure (a signal type with registered callbacks and a reason) is exactly what you build here, sized to the need; one flag per operation tree plus a broadcast is the whole mechanism, and the check costs one relaxed atomic load per safe point. Keep the flag in the token struct, never in a global, and document the contract that operations must not linger in uninterruptible syscalls.
pitfalls: A plain bool or volatile flag shared across threads is a data race; use atomic_bool/atomic_flag, and from a signal handler only a lock-free atomic or sig_atomic_t (and never cnd_broadcast, which is not async-signal-safe).

A blocking syscall without a timeout (read, recv, accept, a bare cnd_wait) never reaches a safe point: use poll/select/ppoll with a timeout, timed waits that re-check, or a self-pipe to deliver the wakeup.
The token must be initialised per operation and its lifetime must cover every user; a flag on the stack that is flipped from another thread after its scope ends is a use-after-free.
Mixing pthread_cancel into code that also uses a token gives two cancellation systems - deferred cancellation points can fire inside a library and run cleanup handlers at unexpected places.

variants.name: POSIX deferred cancellation (pthread_cancel)
variants.implementation_notes: POSIX itself has a cancellation mechanism, but it is attached to the thread, not to an operation: pthread_cancel requests cancellation, PTHREAD_CANCEL_DEFERRED (the default type) delivers it only at cancellation points - functions like read, write, sleep and pthread_testcancel - and cleanup handlers plus pthread_cleanup_push/pop unwind resources. That makes it the POSIX analogue of the pattern for libraries written to be cancel-safe (each thread disables cancelability around critical sections with pthread_setcancelstate and restores it after), and C++-style RAII code that never expects asynchronous exceptions should stay away from it. PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS is forced termination and must not be used around code that touches shared state.
pitfalls: The cancelability state and type live on the thread: a library that enables cancelability while its caller disabled it turns a pending request into cancellation at the wrong place - save and restore the state instead of overwriting it.

Only functions that are cancel-safe may run inside an asynchronously cancellable thread; even in deferred mode, a cancellation point in the middle of a compound update leaves partial state unless cleanup handlers restore the invariant.
pthread_cancel returns immediately but the thread may still be running: join and synchronise before freeing anything the thread uses, or conditionally wait for the cancellation to complete.

There is no reason and no propagation: cancelling a parent thread does not cancel the threads it started - the tree must be cancelled explicitly, which is exactly the bookkeeping a token would centralise.
